The excerpt explicitly says Microsoft Clarity can be used to "validate your assumptions" and "validate your hypothesis."
Moving testimonials higher is supported for the stated example, where they are in the middle or bottom of the site and only 30% of users reach them.
The candidate's trigger presents the 30% example as the operative condition but omits the adjacent placement condition that the testimonials are lower on the page.

The formal depends_on relation to the separate principle is not stated as a procedural or required dependency in the excerpt; the passage supplies it as rationale rather than an explicit prerequisite.
The principle accurately restates the excerpt's assertion that people see less information as they progress farther down the page.
The excerpt demonstrates selecting the Area view, using "edit areas," selecting areas of interest, and viewing the percentage of clicks directed to page elements.

The excerpt describes a live example in which a browsing-menu element looked clickable but was not, received 46% of clicks, caused frustration in recordings and user tests, and was followed by users leaving the site.
The source explicitly recommends using area-map data to consider reorganizing information and to identify redundant, very-low-click sections that can be removed to simplify the experience.
The dependency on area-map data is directly supported by the passage's reference to taking data from the area map.

For the described product-page example, the excerpt explicitly concludes that the large text is too long and "needs to be cut down substantially" so users can scroll down and complete the intended action.
The 25%, 93%, and approximate 30% values are retained as observations from that example rather than recast as general numerical thresholds.
The excerpt supports the warning for an example where a generic top-of-page contact heading precedes a form placed further down the page, making the heading redundant and wasting space.
The candidate's broad title generalizes the warning to B2B contact pages while its trigger omits the material circumstance that the form is further down the page.
The approximately 25% immediate drop-off is an observation from one website example, not a stated general condition for treating generic contact headings as wasted real estate.
The excerpt identifies content engagement as a heat-map and scroll-map use case and states that content can be reorganized based on what users should see.
The excerpt directly advises examining the most frequently clicked navigation elements and says this can help optimize site structure.
The source says to assess whether fundamental CTAs receive clicks and, if not, consider more emphasis, higher placement, or different placements and designs.
The source supports simplifying forms and says that four fields or fewer is "typically the sweet point," but the candidate turns this qualified observation into an unqualified universal instruction.

The candidate's exclusion is logically reversed: "phone number ... is not absolutely necessary" is presented in the source as a reason to remove the field, whereas an exclusion would indicate that the action should not apply in that situation.
The source describes phone-number drop-off and form-entry analysis as observations and questions; it does not make both of them mandatory prerequisites for simplifying every form.
The excerpt clearly supports analyzing the user journey to checkout.

The candidate also specifies a journey to "cart," but the supplied transcript says "apart" at that point. Although this may be a transcription error, the excerpt itself does not reliably establish the candidate's expansion to cart.

The excerpt explicitly recommends assessing whether elements are clearly organized from top to bottom, guide users appropriately, and are effectively designed, including banners, promotional sections, and badges.
The source instructs the user to click recordings and states that recordings can show how long someone spends on the site and where they are coming from.
